## Introduction

A “four-day work week” can mean fewer paid hours at unchanged pay, forty hours compressed into four long shifts, or a partial reduction spread across the week. These are different interventions. A claim that one improves health or output cannot automatically be transferred to another. The distinction matters because the most visible recent pilots generally promise less work time, whereas much of the older four-day literature tested four ten-hour days. Historical studies examined employees' acceptance, reactions, and public-sector attitudes toward those compressed arrangements (Martin, 1981) (Fottler, 1977) (Lacapra, 1973) (Kenny, 1974) (Hodge & Tellier, 1975). The recent growth of four-day schedules in labor-force data also says little by itself about which version workers received (Hamermesh & Biddle, 2022).

This narrative review asks what the research evidence says about productivity, wellbeing, and retention under four-day work weeks. Its central conclusion is uneven: evidence of better short-term wellbeing under paid hours reduction is comparatively persuasive; reports of maintained output are encouraging but less well measured; evidence of fewer employee exits is still limited. The intervention's effect also depends on work intensity, staffing and the use employees can make of freed time. Direct trial evidence is read alongside occupational-health research and studies of compressed schedules, but the latter are identified as different designs rather than pooled into one effect. (Fan et al., 2025) (Utzet et al., 2026) (Bernstrøm et al., 2025)

## Retention

Retention has to be measured as actual employee departures, not willingness to stay, enthusiasm for a schedule, or an employer's decision to keep the policy. Lewis and colleagues’ UK pilot report reported resignations per hundred employees falling from 2.0 in a comparison period to 0.8 during the pilot, a 57% decline. The report itself cautioned that small counts and labor-market conditions prevented a statistically firm causal conclusion. The participating firms were self-selected, and the comparison was historical rather than a matched control group. The figure is therefore suggestive, not an established treatment effect.

Other evidence is about attraction or commitment rather than exits. A conference study of full-time, compressed four-day schedules found that burnout risk predicted preference more clearly than job satisfaction, and that a four-day-week offer increased organizational commitment in a vignette experiment (du Bois et al., 2025). That result identifies a plausible retention pathway for compressed schedules but does not show that fewer employees resigned under a paid hours reduction. Australian early adopters described the schedule as a recruitment and retention tool (Hopkins et al., 2026). Spanish managers likewise named talent attraction and retention among adoption motives (Gallego-Gómez & Parente, 2026). Portuguese leaders perceived strategic value but disagreed about how feasible and durable the model would be (Fontes et al., 2026). These are managerial accounts, not independent turnover estimates.

A four-month pilot among volunteer hospital leaders reported lower burnout and higher job satisfaction, with no observed deterioration in selected patient-safety measures; it did not establish an effect on actual turnover (Hayakawa et al., 2025). A study of front-line service workers linked satisfaction with compressed hours to lower subsequent absenteeism, which is relevant to staffing stability but is not retention and concerns a different schedule (Deery et al., 2016). Early research on compressed weeks documented employee acceptance and favorable reactions (Fottler, 1977) (Hodge & Tellier, 1975). Those historical attitudes show that schedule preference can be measured; they cannot substitute for personnel-record evidence about current paid hours reductions. The research basis for a causal retention benefit is consequently thinner than the basis for short-term wellbeing gains.

## Wellbeing

The wellbeing evidence is broader and methodologically stronger. Fan and colleagues compared before-and-after data for 2,896 employees in 141 organizations adopting a paid four-day reduction with data from twelve comparison companies. Burnout, job satisfaction and self-reported mental and physical health improved in the intervention organizations, a pattern not observed in the comparisons. Larger individual reductions in hours were associated with larger wellbeing improvements, and changes in work ability, sleep problems and fatigue statistically mediated the association (Fan et al., 2025). The comparison firms strengthen inference, but employer participation and worker outcomes were not randomized.

A controlled Swedish public-sector intervention reduced weekly hours by a quarter at unchanged pay. Across 33 randomized workplaces, diary data from 580 participants showed better sleep, less sleepiness and less perceived stress at eighteen months; the reported effects were small (Schiller et al., 2016). A related randomized time-use analysis found lower total workload and more recovery activities during workdays (Schiller et al., 2017). These analyses draw on a related intervention population and should not be counted as independent replications. A separate Swedish social-service quasi-experiment reported improvement in stress, exhaustion, sleep and work intrusion into private life after hours and workload were reduced together (Barck-Holst et al., 2015). Mixed-methods follow-up found less emotional exhaustion but persistent high caseloads, making it difficult to attribute all benefits to hours alone (Barck-Holst et al., 2019). Interviews in that setting emphasized improved off-work recovery and family relationships (Barck-Holst et al., 2020).

Review evidence agrees on direction while limiting certainty. A scoping review of paid hours reduction mapped improvements in work–life balance and mental health, but emphasized heterogeneous schedules, few long-term studies and limited sector coverage (Utzet et al., 2026). A four-day-week people-management review found favorable satisfaction and work–life-balance patterns among the small set of papers it examined, while calling for more organization-level evidence (Araújo et al., 2024). These syntheses overlap with primary studies above, so their positive conclusions should not be treated as additional independent trials. An exploratory Italian study also reported positive individual and organizational wellbeing assessments, while stressing the need to examine how work is evaluated and organized (Antonelli & Luciano, 2025).

## Discussion

The evidence is most coherent when the treatment is defined by paid hours, pay, workload and shift length. The favorable reduced-hours results can coexist with mixed compressed-week results because four longer days may increase fatigue even when a fifth commuting day disappears (Utzet et al., 2026) (Bernstrøm et al., 2025). Mechanisms also vary: recovery and motivation may protect performance (Rae & Russell, 2025) (Pencavel, 2016), but intensified monitoring and workload can offset some of the time benefit (Delaney & Casey, 2021). Studies of social workers demonstrate that cutting workload alongside hours is part of the intervention, not a nuisance detail (Barck-Holst et al., 2015) (Barck-Holst et al., 2019). A case study of a small Hungarian firm adds that usable free time depends on other people's schedules (Venczel, 2024).

The wider policy literature raises questions beyond the firm-level average. Social-policy scholarship frames the four-day week as a distributional question (Chung, 2022); research on shorter full-time standards examines gender equality in paid and care work (Kümmerling, 2026). A recent interview study suggests that a day away from paid work can be filled with unpaid obligations unequally (Cruz & Hoth, 2026). Studies of environmental consequences (Cieplinski et al., 2021) and employment effects (Booth & Schiantarelli, 1987) address different endpoints. An SSRN analysis of four-day-week discourse (Lehmann et al., 2024) and broader accounts of implementation (Frayne et al., 2024) (Hong et al., 2024) help explain why advocacy, law and organizational experiments often use the same label for different arrangements. None of these contextual works should be mistaken for direct evidence on output or exits.

Qualitative and survey research exposes important exceptions. A New Zealand financial-services case study found that staff welcomed the policy yet experienced stronger performance monitoring and productivity pressure (Delaney & Casey, 2021). A small Hungarian study found that wellbeing gains depended on time for personally meaningful activities, not merely nominal release from work (Venczel, 2024). Interviews with women in a childcare nonprofit described how freed time could be absorbed by unequal care obligations (Cruz & Hoth, 2026). In the UAE's four-and-a-half-day survey, many respondents reported better work–life balance, but more than a third reported increased weekday stress; the sample was concentrated in public education and was not representative (Alawad & Smail, 2026). A qualitative UK study of workers still on five-day schedules raised similar anticipated concerns about workload and coordination; these were expectations, not measured implementation effects (Jain et al., 2025). Across these studies, hours saved, work intensity and household demands jointly shape wellbeing.

## Productivity

A work week can become more productive per hour while producing the same, more, or less in total. This distinction is often blurred. In a historical munitions dataset, Pencavel found a nonlinear output-hours relationship: output rose at a diminishing rate beyond an hours threshold (Pencavel, 2014). A separate study modeled both fatigue and learning effects across working-hour thresholds (Lee & Lim, 2017). These studies make it plausible that cutting low-yield hours can preserve output, but neither measured a contemporary four-day-week rollout. Recovery-based theory similarly proposes that a shorter week may improve subsequent performance through rest (Pencavel, 2016). The cognitive-science argument for recovery and motivation is a mechanism hypothesis, not a trial result (Rae & Russell, 2025).

Direct employer evidence is more provisional. In Lewis and colleagues’ UK pilot report, revenue among the firms supplying start-to-end data rose by 1.4% on a company-size-weighted basis; the participating organizations had adopted a variety of shorter-hours arrangements. Revenue is an imperfect proxy for productivity, only a subset supplied the figures, and the pilot lacked a comparable nonadopting-firm series. The Australian early-adopter study identified reported productivity gains and workflow changes, but its qualitative design cannot isolate an output effect (Hopkins et al., 2026). Spanish managers described efficiency as a motivation for adoption and recommended clear performance indicators; an intention to become more efficient is not observed efficiency (Gallego-Gómez & Parente, 2026). A four-day-week review reports favorable productivity findings among the small number of organizational papers it examined while noting the shortage of organization-level research (Araújo et al., 2024).

Another distinction is between expectations and realized performance. Belgian listed firms had positive average stock-price reactions around the announcement of a compressed-week law, particularly among firms with more knowledge work or lower prior employee productivity (Dutordoir & Struyfs, 2024). Investors' expectations do not establish an eventual production gain. A policy analysis of Australian productivity advocates a four-day week, but an argument for adoption is also not a measured treatment effect (Blackham, 2025). Nor should a study of changing national days-of-work patterns be read as an evaluation of firms adopting reduced hours (Hamermesh & Biddle, 2022).

# 4 Day Work Week: What the Trials Actually Measured

## 4 Day Work Week: What the Trials Actually Measured

The best evidence on the four-day work week says it improves how workers feel: lower burnout, better sleep, less fatigue. In the firms that reported revenue (23 out of 61 in the largest UK pilot), output mostly held steady. But no trial was randomized, every participating company volunteered, and most outcomes were self-reported. The version of "four-day week" matters too: 32 hours at full pay is a different intervention than 40 hours crammed into four 10-hour days. At the far end of the scale, see what working 80 hours a week costs.

**Key takeaways:**

- The two biggest trials (UK 2022 and Fan et al. 2025) measured well-being, not productivity. Revenue data came from fewer than half the UK firms.
- Every major trial used self-selected companies. The authors of Fan et al. say their findings likely overestimate the true effect.
- A "4 day work week" can mean 32 hours at full pay (the 100-80-100 model) or a compressed 4x10 schedule. The health and focus implications are different.
- The firms that succeeded did not just delete Friday. They cut meetings, moved communication async, and protected focus time first.

### Limitations

This review is narrative, with no formal screening or pooled effect estimate. Thirty-eight DOI sources were read at abstract level and twelve at metadata level; none was marked as full-text read in the source corpus. Metadata-only works inform the scope map only. The UK pilot report has no DOI in the retrieved record and is linked by name; its bibliographic status was not checked by the DOI script. A resolved DOI establishes that a work exists, not that a claim is supported; claim checks here were limited by accessible abstracts and the separately read pilot report. The literature itself is constrained by self-selection, short follow-up, heterogeneous interventions and limited objective output and turnover measures. No unresolved DOI or unverifiable empirical claim is carried into the outcome synthesis.

## Conclusion

Paid reductions to a four-day week are associated with better short-term wellbeing in multi-organization pilots and controlled hours-reduction studies. Evidence that output can be maintained in some adopting firms is plausible but relies heavily on incomplete firm reports and indirect productivity measures. The proposed retention benefit is promising yet rests mainly on pilot turnover comparisons, organizational accounts and commitment measures rather than controlled personnel-record evidence. Compressed forty-hour weeks have a different, mixed evidence base. Future evaluations should record actual paid hours, workload, output quality, costs and employee exits against comparable nonadopters, with attention to sector and household care demands.

## Schedule Definitions and Evidence Map

Reduced-hours studies generally retain pay while cutting paid time; the intervention may shorten each day, remove a day, or rotate time off. Spanish manager interviews document several such designs, including shorter daily hours, Friday closure and rotating schedules (Gallego-Gómez & Parente, 2026). The Australian early-adopter study concerns a 100:80:100 model and reports firm accounts of redesigning workflows, while a Portuguese leadership study examines managerial perceptions of organizational feasibility (Hopkins et al., 2026) (Fontes et al., 2026). Neither estimates the effect of one standard schedule across all employers. A United Arab Emirates survey studied a four-and-a-half-day policy, with perceptions of both recovery and denser weekdays; it is another distinct case (Alawad & Smail, 2026).

By contrast, compression preserves weekly hours and extends shifts. A Belgian event study measures investors' reaction to the announcement of a compressed-week law, not subsequent worker output (Dutordoir & Struyfs, 2024). A Philippine survey models perceptions of stress, work–life balance and productivity under a compressed schedule (Paje et al., 2020); a front-line service study relates satisfaction with compressed hours to later absenteeism (Deery et al., 2016). The longitudinal review of compressed weeks found mixed health and work outcomes, including greater shift satisfaction but possible higher sickness absence. Shift length and the comparison schedule mattered (Bernstrøm et al., 2025). This is a direct reason to resist a single pooled “four-day” estimate.

The wider literature also asks different questions. Studies on weekly hours and job satisfaction (Nanda & Browne, 1977), long hours and health (Hulst, 2003), and work-time control among overtime employees (Yu & Leka, 2022) help explain why time might matter, but none by itself tests a paid four-day reduction. A paper on work-time reduction during pandemic furlough reported gender-differentiated mental-health patterns in that exceptional context (WANG et al., 2022). It should inform caution about distributional effects, rather than serve as a trial of a modern four-day policy.

## So, Does the 4 Day Work Week Work?

For well-being in volunteer, mostly white-collar firms: yes, consistently. Burnout drops, sleep improves, fatigue falls, people stay longer.

For output and revenue: probably neutral in the firms that tried it, but the data is thin (23 firms), self-reported, and drawn from companies already optimistic about the idea.

For everyone: unproven. Hourly workers, shift workers, and industries with hard coverage requirements were mostly absent. And the compressed 4x10, which is what many employers actually mean by "four-day week," is a different intervention with different trade-offs. The version matters more than the label.

## What Is a 4 Day Work Week? Two Models, Not One

The phrase "4 day work week" describes two structurally different schedules.

**The 100-80-100 model** means 100% pay, 80% time, 100% expected output. Workers drop to about 32 hours across four days. This is what the UK pilot and Fan et al. tested.

**The compressed 4x10 schedule** keeps total hours at 40 but packs them into four 10-hour days. Tokyo's Metropolitan Government adopted this model in April 2025, allowing staff to take three days off per week under a flexible system with total monthly hours of 155. Same hours, rearranged.

In the US, the Thirty-Two-Hour Workweek Act (S. 3947) was introduced in March 2024 by Senators Sanders and Butler. It would lower the FLSA overtime threshold from 40 to 32 hours in phases. It has been introduced. It is not law.

The health trade-offs diverge between models. Bambra's 2008 review of compressed schedules found that work-life balance improved, but the studies were low quality and outcomes mostly self-reported. A 10-hour day can bring fatigue that a 32-hour week avoids.

## Methodology

This is a narrative literature review. Searches through Crossref and OpenAlex covered “four-day workweek,” “shorter working week,” “working time reduction,” “compressed workweek,” productivity, health, and turnover, with follow-up queries for named studies and mechanisms. Fifty distinct DOI records were resolved against Crossref or DataCite. Their abstracts were retrieved where available, and records without accessible content were used only to map the literature, not to report findings. A UK pilot report without a retrieved DOI was read separately as grey literature and is identified by name and link when discussed. Selection prioritized direct interventions and reviews; older work on hours and output supplied context. The synthesis compared schedule design, evidence type and outcome measure, without treating a survey, administrative series and vignette experiment as interchangeable observations.

One global HR-outcomes evaluation was retained in the scope map, although its content was unavailable for outcome synthesis (Adediran, 2025). The mapped literature includes chronological and sustainability reviews (de Araujo & Venz, 2025) (Campbell, 2023), work-time policy arguments (Frayne et al., 2024) (Chung, 2022) (Hong et al., 2024), economic analyses of employment and distribution (Booth & Schiantarelli, 1987) (Corneo, 1995), and environmental analyses of reduced hours (Zhang et al., 2026) (Cieplinski et al., 2021). These works define the field's scope rather than establish effects on the three outcomes examined here. Some accounts discuss public services and labor-law implementation without evaluating individual outcomes (Blackham, 2025) (Kümmerling, 2026) (Hopkins et al., 2026). This distinction between background scholarship and outcome evidence governs the claims below.

## The Big Trials at a Glance

| Trial | Who | Hours Change | What Was Measured | Headline Result | Main Limitation | 
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **UK pilot (2022)** | 61 UK organizations, ~2,900 workers | 40 to ~32 hrs (20% cut) | Self-reported burnout, stress, sick days; revenue for 23 firms | 71% lower burnout; revenue +1.4% avg (23 firms) | No control group; firms self-selected through advocacy org | 
| **Fan et al. (2025)** | 141 organizations, 2,896 workers, 6 countries | 39.21 to 34.01 hrs avg (~13% cut) | Burnout, job satisfaction, mental/physical health | Burnout dropped from 2.83 to 2.38 (1-5 scale) | Not randomized; 12 control companies only; self-selected sample | 
| **Iceland (2015-2019)** | 2,500+ public-sector workers | 40 to 35-36 hrs | Well-being, service provision, work-life balance | Maintained or improved service; 86% of workforce later moved to shorter hours or gained the right to them | Five shorter days, not four; public sector only | 
| **Microsoft Japan (2019)** | One company, one month (August) | 5 Fridays off | Sales per employee vs Aug 2018 | +39.9% sales per employee | Company-reported; one month; concurrent 30-min meeting cap | 
| **Bambra (2008)** | 40 studies of compressed weeks | Same total hours, fewer days | Self-reported health, work-life balance | No detrimental effect on self-reported health in 5 controlled studies; work-life balance improved | Mostly self-reported; low methodological quality across studies |

## What Did the UK Four-Day Week Trial Actually Find?

From June to December 2022, 61 UK organizations and about 2,900 employees participated in a six-month pilot studied by researchers at the University of Cambridge and Boston College with the think tank Autonomy. Workers took a 20% reduction in hours with no reduction in pay.

The results, by the numbers:

- **71%** of employees self-reported lower burnout
- **39%** said they were less stressed compared to the start of the trial
- **65%** reduction in sick days vs. the same period the prior year
- **57%** fall in staff turnover vs. the same period the prior year
- **Revenue** rose 1.4% on average, but only**23 of 61 organizations** provided revenue data. That denominator matters.
- **56 of 61** companies (92%) intended to continue; 18 confirmed the policy as permanent

One year later, the follow-up was strong. Autonomy's "Making It Stick" report found at least 54 of 61 firms (89%) were still operating a four-day week, and at least 31 (51%) had made it permanent.

What this trial did not have: a control group. Every firm entered voluntarily through an advocacy organization. The 92% continuation figure tells you something about these specific firms, not about all firms.

## The Biggest Study Yet: 141 Companies in Six Countries

Fan, Schor, Kelly, and Gu (2025), published in *Nature Human Behaviour*, followed 2,896 employees across 141 organizations in six countries through a six-month trial. Twelve companies served as controls.

Average company hours fell from **39.21 to 34.01 per week**, a cut of about 13%, not the full 20% the label implies. Work burnout fell from **2.83 to 2.38** on a 1-to-5 scale. Job satisfaction, mental health, and physical health all improved. The control companies showed no comparable changes.

The mediators: self-reported work ability improved, sleep problems fell, fatigue decreased. The gains were not about more output per hour. They were about less damage per week.

The authors are explicit about the limits. Firms were recruited through 4 Day Week Global, an advocacy organization. The sample is mostly white-collar. The authors themselves write that their findings likely overestimate the true effect.

## Iceland's "Four-Day Week" Was Actually a 35-to-36-Hour Week

The Iceland trials, run by Reykjavík City Council and the national government from 2015 to 2019, involved more than 2,500 workers, about 1% of the Icelandic workforce. Hours dropped from 40 to 35 or 36 at the same pay.

For many participants, that meant five shorter days, not four. Calling it a "four-day week" is media shorthand.

Service provision was maintained or improved, and well-being rose. The political impact was large: according to Autonomy and the Association for Sustainable Democracy (Alda), about 86% of Iceland's workforce has since moved to shorter hours or gained the right to negotiate them. A policy success, but one about reducing weekly hours, not about a specific day off.

## Does a 4 Day Work Week Increase Productivity?

This is the question everyone asks, and the answer is less clean than the headlines suggest.

**Microsoft Japan** gave employees five Fridays off in August 2019, capped meetings at 30 minutes, and pushed communication online. Sales per employee rose 39.9% versus August 2018. But this was one company, one month, with concurrent process changes. A case study, not a controlled experiment.

The broader evidence on hours and output is older but stronger. Economist John Pencavel, analyzing data on British munitions workers from World War I, found that below about 49 hours per week, output was roughly proportional to hours. Above that, returns diminished sharply. Cutting from 55 to 40 costs less output than you would expect. Cutting from 40 to 32 is a different question, and Pencavel's data does not answer it.

A 2021 WHO/ILO study estimated that working 55+ hours per week led to 745,000 deaths from stroke and ischemic heart disease in 2016: 35% higher stroke risk, 17% higher heart disease mortality versus 35-to-40-hour weeks. That is the case against long weeks, not proof that shorter weeks improve output.

Taken together, the observed firm reports are consistent with output being maintained in some workplaces. They do not justify a general claim that a four-day week raises aggregate productivity. Service quality, staffing costs, work shifted to nonparticipants and output per paid hour need to be measured together. The case for a gain is strongest where organizations can remove low-value meetings or reallocate work and weakest where continuous coverage requires replacement labor; the retrieved employee interviews identify coordination and workload concerns in such roles (Jain et al., 2025). Contextual work on hours, productivity and job satisfaction points to mechanisms worth measuring, not a universal effect size (Nanda & Browne, 1977) (Lee & Lim, 2017).

## 4 Day Work Week Pros and Cons

| Pros (supported by trial data) | Cons and unknowns | 
|---|---|
| Lower self-reported burnout (UK: 71%; Fan et al.: 2.83 to 2.38 on 5-point scale) | All major trials used self-selected firms; no randomization | 
| Better sleep and reduced fatigue (Fan et al. mediators) | Most outcomes self-reported, not independently measured | 
| 65% fewer sick days in UK pilot | Revenue data from only 23 of 61 UK firms | 
| 57% less staff turnover in UK pilot | Compressed 4x10 carries fatigue and childcare trade-offs | 
| Improved work-life balance across trials | Hourly and shift workers are underrepresented in samples | 
| High retention: 89% of UK firms still on it at one year | Customer-facing and coverage-dependent roles face scheduling gaps | 
| Bambra review: compressed weeks improved work-life balance | Bambra review: studies were low quality, mostly self-reported | 

## What the Trials Changed Before They Cut the Day

The companies that made four-day weeks work did not just cross Friday off the calendar. They redesigned how work happened first.

Microsoft Japan capped meetings at 30 minutes. Fan et al. describe "pre-trial work reorganization" in which companies improved efficiency and collaboration before the six-month clock started. The common thread: fewer meetings, async communication, and protected focus blocks. These are the changes Parkinson's law predicts: work expands to fill the time, so when you cut the time, you cut the filler.

Whether your company runs four days or five, the practical lesson is the same. Your output tracks your focused hours, not your logged hours. Protecting two or three deep work blocks per day from meetings and interruptions is the part of these trials any schedule can copy, even if the headline was about the missing Friday. For more on guarding those blocks, see what context switching actually costs and timeboxing your focus hours.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Is a 4 day work week 32 hours?

Usually, but not always. The 100-80-100 model tested in the UK pilot and Fan et al. means about 32 hours at full pay. A compressed 4x10 schedule keeps total hours at 40. Tokyo's public-sector model uses 155 hours per month. Same label, different hours.

### Which companies have a 4 day work week?

Microsoft Japan trialed it for one month in August 2019. The Tokyo Metropolitan Government began offering a compressed option in April 2025. Beyond those, the best-documented examples are the 61 UK pilot firms (56 intended to continue) and the 141 volunteer organizations in Fan et al., mostly white-collar and recruited through 4 Day Week Global.

### Do you get paid the same on a 4 day work week?

In the 100-80-100 model, yes. Workers take a 20% reduction in hours with no cut in pay. The compressed 4x10 model also preserves full pay since total hours remain at 40. Both the UK pilot and Fan et al. held wages constant.

### Is a 4x10 schedule better than five 8-hour days?

Bambra's 2008 review found that compressed weeks improved work-life balance, but the studies were low quality and outcomes were mostly self-reported. A 10-hour day can bring more fatigue, and childcare logistics can be harder. Whether it is "better" depends on your role, your commute, and how well you sustain focus past hour eight.

### Did productivity drop in the four-day week trials?

Revenue in the 23 UK firms that reported it rose 1.4% on average. Fan et al. measured well-being, not revenue. Microsoft Japan's 39.9% jump was one company, one month, with concurrent changes. Output mostly held steady where measured, but it was not measured in most trials.

### Is the US moving to a 32-hour work week?

The Thirty-Two-Hour Workweek Act (S. 3947) was introduced in the Senate in March 2024. It would phase the FLSA overtime threshold down from 40 to 32 hours. It has not advanced beyond introduction and is not law. No federal policy change is imminent as of 2026.

## Four Days Only Work If the Focus Hours Hold

The trials did not just delete a day. They cut meetings, moved communication async, and built protected focus time into the remaining hours. The well-being gains tracked through less fatigue and better work ability, not through some abstract productivity multiplier.

That is the part that transfers to any schedule: your output depends on how many of your hours are genuinely focused, not how many hours you log. On a compressed 4x10, or a standard five-day week, or an actual 32-hour week, the bottleneck is the same.

Roon is built for those focus blocks. The duration comes from methylliberine slowing caffeine's clearance: in a randomized crossover study (n=12), co-administration cut caffeine's oral clearance from 41.9 to 17.1 L/hr and extended its half-life from 7.2 to 15 hours, with no increase in peak concentration. A study of front-line service workers linked satisfaction with compressed hours to lower subsequent absenteeism, which is relevant to staffing stability but is not retention and concerns a different schedule (Deery et al., 2016). Early research on compressed weeks documented employee acceptance and favorable reactions (Fottler, 1977) (Hodge & Tellier, 1975). Those historical attitudes show that schedule preference can be measured; they cannot substitute for personnel-record evidence about current paid hours reductions. The research basis for a causal retention benefit is consequently thinner than the basis for short-term wellbeing gains.

## Wellbeing

The wellbeing evidence is broader and methodologically stronger. Fan and colleagues compared before-and-after data for 2,896 employees in 141 organizations adopting a paid four-day reduction with data from twelve comparison companies. Burnout, job satisfaction and self-reported mental and physical health improved in the intervention organizations, a pattern not observed in the comparisons. Larger individual reductions in hours were associated with larger wellbeing improvements, and changes in work ability, sleep problems and fatigue statistically mediated the association (Fan et al., 2025). The comparison firms strengthen inference, but employer participation and worker outcomes were not randomized.

A controlled Swedish public-sector intervention reduced weekly hours by a quarter at unchanged pay. Across 33 randomized workplaces, diary data from 580 participants showed better sleep, less sleepiness and less perceived stress at eighteen months; the reported effects were small (Schiller et al., 2016). A related randomized time-use analysis found lower total workload and more recovery activities during workdays (Schiller et al., 2017). These analyses draw on a related intervention population and should not be counted as independent replications. A separate Swedish social-service quasi-experiment reported improvement in stress, exhaustion, sleep and work intrusion into private life after hours and workload were reduced together (Barck-Holst et al., 2015). Mixed-methods follow-up found less emotional exhaustion but persistent high caseloads, making it difficult to attribute all benefits to hours alone (Barck-Holst et al., 2019). Interviews in that setting emphasized improved off-work recovery and family relationships (Barck-Holst et al., 2020).

Review evidence agrees on direction while limiting certainty. A scoping review of paid hours reduction mapped improvements in work–life balance and mental health, but emphasized heterogeneous schedules, few long-term studies and limited sector coverage (Utzet et al., 2026). A four-day-week people-management review found favorable satisfaction and work–life-balance patterns among the small set of papers it examined, while calling for more organization-level evidence (Araújo et al., 2024). These syntheses overlap with primary studies above, so their positive conclusions should not be treated as additional independent trials. An exploratory Italian study also reported positive individual and organizational wellbeing assessments, while stressing the need to examine how work is evaluated and organized (Antonelli & Luciano, 2025).

## Discussion

The evidence is most coherent when the treatment is defined by paid hours, pay, workload and shift length. The favorable reduced-hours results can coexist with mixed compressed-week results because four longer days may increase fatigue even when a fifth commuting day disappears (Utzet et al., 2026) (Bernstrøm et al., 2025). Mechanisms also vary: recovery and motivation may protect performance (Rae & Russell, 2025) (Pencavel, 2016), but intensified monitoring and workload can offset some of the time benefit (Delaney & Casey, 2021). Studies of social workers demonstrate that cutting workload alongside hours is part of the intervention, not a nuisance detail (Barck-Holst et al., 2015) (Barck-Holst et al., 2019). A case study of a small Hungarian firm adds that usable free time depends on other people's schedules (Venczel, 2024).

The wider policy literature raises questions beyond the firm-level average. Social-policy scholarship frames the four-day week as a distributional question (Chung, 2022); research on shorter full-time standards examines gender equality in paid and care work (Kümmerling, 2026). A recent interview study suggests that a day away from paid work can be filled with unpaid obligations unequally (Cruz & Hoth, 2026). Studies of environmental consequences (Cieplinski et al., 2021) and employment effects (Booth & Schiantarelli, 1987) address different endpoints. An SSRN analysis of four-day-week discourse (Lehmann et al., 2024) and broader accounts of implementation (Frayne et al., 2024) (Hong et al., 2024) help explain why advocacy, law and organizational experiments often use the same label for different arrangements. None of these contextual works should be mistaken for direct evidence on output or exits.

Qualitative and survey research exposes important exceptions. A New Zealand financial-services case study found that staff welcomed the policy yet experienced stronger performance monitoring and productivity pressure (Delaney & Casey, 2021). A small Hungarian study found that wellbeing gains depended on time for personally meaningful activities, not merely nominal release from work (Venczel, 2024). Interviews with women in a childcare nonprofit described how freed time could be absorbed by unequal care obligations (Cruz & Hoth, 2026). In the UAE's four-and-a-half-day survey, many respondents reported better work–life balance, but more than a third reported increased weekday stress; the sample was concentrated in public education and was not representative (Alawad & Smail, 2026). A qualitative UK study of workers still on five-day schedules raised similar anticipated concerns about workload and coordination; these were expectations, not measured implementation effects (Jain et al., 2025). Across these studies, hours saved, work intensity and household demands jointly shape wellbeing.

## Productivity

A work week can become more productive per hour while producing the same, more, or less in total. This distinction is often blurred. In a historical munitions dataset, Pencavel found a nonlinear output-hours relationship: output rose at a diminishing rate beyond an hours threshold (Pencavel, 2014). A separate study modeled both fatigue and learning effects across working-hour thresholds (Lee & Lim, 2017). These studies make it plausible that cutting low-yield hours can preserve output, but neither measured a contemporary four-day-week rollout. Recovery-based theory similarly proposes that a shorter week may improve subsequent performance through rest (Pencavel, 2016). The cognitive-science argument for recovery and motivation is a mechanism hypothesis, not a trial result (Rae & Russell, 2025).

Direct employer evidence is more provisional. In Lewis and colleagues’ UK pilot report, revenue among the firms supplying start-to-end data rose by 1.4% on a company-size-weighted basis; the participating organizations had adopted a variety of shorter-hours arrangements. Revenue is an imperfect proxy for productivity, only a subset supplied the figures, and the pilot lacked a comparable nonadopting-firm series. The Australian early-adopter study identified reported productivity gains and workflow changes, but its qualitative design cannot isolate an output effect (Hopkins et al., 2026). Spanish managers described efficiency as a motivation for adoption and recommended clear performance indicators; an intention to become more efficient is not observed efficiency (Gallego-Gómez & Parente, 2026). A four-day-week review reports favorable productivity findings among the small number of organizational papers it examined while noting the shortage of organization-level research (Araújo et al., 2024).

Another distinction is between expectations and realized performance. Belgian listed firms had positive average stock-price reactions around the announcement of a compressed-week law, particularly among firms with more knowledge work or lower prior employee productivity (Dutordoir & Struyfs, 2024). Investors' expectations do not establish an eventual production gain. A policy analysis of Australian productivity advocates a four-day week, but an argument for adoption is also not a measured treatment effect (Blackham, 2025). Nor should a study of changing national days-of-work patterns be read as an evaluation of firms adopting reduced hours (Hamermesh & Biddle, 2022).

# 4 Day Work Week: What the Trials Actually Measured

## 4 Day Work Week: What the Trials Actually Measured

The best evidence on the four-day work week says it improves how workers feel: lower burnout, better sleep, less fatigue. In the firms that reported revenue (23 out of 61 in the largest UK pilot), output mostly held steady. But no trial was randomized, every participating company volunteered, and most outcomes were self-reported. The version of "four-day week" matters too: 32 hours at full pay is a different intervention than 40 hours crammed into four 10-hour days. At the far end of the scale, see what working 80 hours a week costs.

**Key takeaways:**

- The two biggest trials (UK 2022 and Fan et al. 2025) measured well-being, not productivity. Revenue data came from fewer than half the UK firms.
- Every major trial used self-selected companies. The authors of Fan et al. say their findings likely overestimate the true effect.
- A "4 day work week" can mean 32 hours at full pay (the 100-80-100 model) or a compressed 4x10 schedule. The health and focus implications are different.
- The firms that succeeded did not just delete Friday. They cut meetings, moved communication async, and protected focus time first.

### Limitations

This review is narrative, with no formal screening or pooled effect estimate. Thirty-eight DOI sources were read at abstract level and twelve at metadata level; none was marked as full-text read in the source corpus. Metadata-only works inform the scope map only. The UK pilot report has no DOI in the retrieved record and is linked by name; its bibliographic status was not checked by the DOI script. A resolved DOI establishes that a work exists, not that a claim is supported; claim checks here were limited by accessible abstracts and the separately read pilot report. The literature itself is constrained by self-selection, short follow-up, heterogeneous interventions and limited objective output and turnover measures. No unresolved DOI or unverifiable empirical claim is carried into the outcome synthesis.

## Conclusion

Paid reductions to a four-day week are associated with better short-term wellbeing in multi-organization pilots and controlled hours-reduction studies. Evidence that output can be maintained in some adopting firms is plausible but relies heavily on incomplete firm reports and indirect productivity measures. The proposed retention benefit is promising yet rests mainly on pilot turnover comparisons, organizational accounts and commitment measures rather than controlled personnel-record evidence. Compressed forty-hour weeks have a different, mixed evidence base. Future evaluations should record actual paid hours, workload, output quality, costs and employee exits against comparable nonadopters, with attention to sector and household care demands.

## Schedule Definitions and Evidence Map

Reduced-hours studies generally retain pay while cutting paid time; the intervention may shorten each day, remove a day, or rotate time off. Spanish manager interviews document several such designs, including shorter daily hours, Friday closure and rotating schedules (Gallego-Gómez & Parente, 2026). The Australian early-adopter study concerns a 100:80:100 model and reports firm accounts of redesigning workflows, while a Portuguese leadership study examines managerial perceptions of organizational feasibility (Hopkins et al., 2026) (Fontes et al., 2026). Neither estimates the effect of one standard schedule across all employers. A United Arab Emirates survey studied a four-and-a-half-day policy, with perceptions of both recovery and denser weekdays; it is another distinct case (Alawad & Smail, 2026).

By contrast, compression preserves weekly hours and extends shifts. A Belgian event study measures investors' reaction to the announcement of a compressed-week law, not subsequent worker output (Dutordoir & Struyfs, 2024). A Philippine survey models perceptions of stress, work–life balance and productivity under a compressed schedule (Paje et al., 2020); a front-line service study relates satisfaction with compressed hours to later absenteeism (Deery et al., 2016). The longitudinal review of compressed weeks found mixed health and work outcomes, including greater shift satisfaction but possible higher sickness absence. Shift length and the comparison schedule mattered (Bernstrøm et al., 2025). This is a direct reason to resist a single pooled “four-day” estimate.

The wider literature also asks different questions. Studies on weekly hours and job satisfaction (Nanda & Browne, 1977), long hours and health (Hulst, 2003), and work-time control among overtime employees (Yu & Leka, 2022) help explain why time might matter, but none by itself tests a paid four-day reduction. A paper on work-time reduction during pandemic furlough reported gender-differentiated mental-health patterns in that exceptional context (WANG et al., 2022). It should inform caution about distributional effects, rather than serve as a trial of a modern four-day policy.

## So, Does the 4 Day Work Week Work?

For well-being in volunteer, mostly white-collar firms: yes, consistently. Burnout drops, sleep improves, fatigue falls, people stay longer.

For output and revenue: probably neutral in the firms that tried it, but the data is thin (23 firms), self-reported, and drawn from companies already optimistic about the idea.

For everyone: unproven. Hourly workers, shift workers, and industries with hard coverage requirements were mostly absent. And the compressed 4x10, which is what many employers actually mean by "four-day week," is a different intervention with different trade-offs. The version matters more than the label.

## What Is a 4 Day Work Week? Two Models, Not One

The phrase "4 day work week" describes two structurally different schedules.

**The 100-80-100 model** means 100% pay, 80% time, 100% expected output. Workers drop to about 32 hours across four days. This is what the UK pilot and Fan et al. tested.

**The compressed 4x10 schedule** keeps total hours at 40 but packs them into four 10-hour days. Tokyo's Metropolitan Government adopted this model in April 2025, allowing staff to take three days off per week under a flexible system with total monthly hours of 155. Same hours, rearranged.

In the US, the Thirty-Two-Hour Workweek Act (S. 3947) was introduced in March 2024 by Senators Sanders and Butler. It would lower the FLSA overtime threshold from 40 to 32 hours in phases. It has been introduced. It is not law.

The health trade-offs diverge between models. Bambra's 2008 review of compressed schedules found that work-life balance improved, but the studies were low quality and outcomes mostly self-reported. A 10-hour day can bring fatigue that a 32-hour week avoids.

## Methodology

This is a narrative literature review. Searches through Crossref and OpenAlex covered “four-day workweek,” “shorter working week,” “working time reduction,” “compressed workweek,” productivity, health, and turnover, with follow-up queries for named studies and mechanisms. Fifty distinct DOI records were resolved against Crossref or DataCite. Their abstracts were retrieved where available, and records without accessible content were used only to map the literature, not to report findings. A UK pilot report without a retrieved DOI was read separately as grey literature and is identified by name and link when discussed. Selection prioritized direct interventions and reviews; older work on hours and output supplied context. The synthesis compared schedule design, evidence type and outcome measure, without treating a survey, administrative series and vignette experiment as interchangeable observations.

One global HR-outcomes evaluation was retained in the scope map, although its content was unavailable for outcome synthesis (Adediran, 2025). The mapped literature includes chronological and sustainability reviews (de Araujo & Venz, 2025) (Campbell, 2023), work-time policy arguments (Frayne et al., 2024) (Chung, 2022) (Hong et al., 2024), economic analyses of employment and distribution (Booth & Schiantarelli, 1987) (Corneo, 1995), and environmental analyses of reduced hours (Zhang et al., 2026) (Cieplinski et al., 2021). These works define the field's scope rather than establish effects on the three outcomes examined here. Some accounts discuss public services and labor-law implementation without evaluating individual outcomes (Blackham, 2025) (Kümmerling, 2026) (Hopkins et al., 2026). This distinction between background scholarship and outcome evidence governs the claims below.

## What Did the UK Four-Day Week Trial Actually Find?

From June to December 2022, 61 UK organizations and about 2,900 employees participated in a six-month pilot studied by researchers at the University of Cambridge and Boston College with the think tank Autonomy. Workers took a 20% reduction in hours with no reduction in pay.

The results, by the numbers:

- **71%** of employees self-reported lower burnout
- **39%** said they were less stressed compared to the start of the trial
- **65%** reduction in sick days vs. the same period the prior year
- **57%** fall in staff turnover vs. the same period the prior year
- **Revenue** rose 1.4% on average, but only**23 of 61 organizations** provided revenue data. That denominator matters.
- **56 of 61** companies (92%) intended to continue; 18 confirmed the policy as permanent

One year later, the follow-up was strong. Autonomy's "Making It Stick" report found at least 54 of 61 firms (89%) were still operating a four-day week, and at least 31 (51%) had made it permanent.

What this trial did not have: a control group. Every firm entered voluntarily through an advocacy organization. The 92% continuation figure tells you something about these specific firms, not about all firms.

## The Biggest Study Yet: 141 Companies in Six Countries

Fan, Schor, Kelly, and Gu (2025), published in *Nature Human Behaviour*, followed 2,896 employees across 141 organizations in six countries through a six-month trial. Twelve companies served as controls.

Average company hours fell from **39.21 to 34.01 per week**, a cut of about 13%, not the full 20% the label implies. Work burnout fell from **2.83 to 2.38** on a 1-to-5 scale. Job satisfaction, mental health, and physical health all improved. The control companies showed no comparable changes.

The mediators: self-reported work ability improved, sleep problems fell, fatigue decreased. The gains were not about more output per hour. They were about less damage per week.

The authors are explicit about the limits. Firms were recruited through 4 Day Week Global, an advocacy organization. The sample is mostly white-collar. The authors themselves write that their findings likely overestimate the true effect.

## Iceland's "Four-Day Week" Was Actually a 35-to-36-Hour Week

The Iceland trials, run by Reykjavík City Council and the national government from 2015 to 2019, involved more than 2,500 workers, about 1% of the Icelandic workforce. Hours dropped from 40 to 35 or 36 at the same pay.

For many participants, that meant five shorter days, not four. Calling it a "four-day week" is media shorthand.

Service provision was maintained or improved, and well-being rose. The political impact was large: according to Autonomy and the Association for Sustainable Democracy (Alda), about 86% of Iceland's workforce has since moved to shorter hours or gained the right to negotiate them. A policy success, but one about reducing weekly hours, not about a specific day off.

## Does a 4 Day Work Week Increase Productivity?

This is the question everyone asks, and the answer is less clean than the headlines suggest.

**Microsoft Japan** gave employees five Fridays off in August 2019, capped meetings at 30 minutes, and pushed communication online. Sales per employee rose 39.9% versus August 2018. But this was one company, one month, with concurrent process changes. A case study, not a controlled experiment.

The broader evidence on hours and output is older but stronger. Economist John Pencavel, analyzing data on British munitions workers from World War I, found that below about 49 hours per week, output was roughly proportional to hours. Above that, returns diminished sharply. Cutting from 55 to 40 costs less output than you would expect. Cutting from 40 to 32 is a different question, and Pencavel's data does not answer it.

A 2021 WHO/ILO study estimated that working 55+ hours per week led to 745,000 deaths from stroke and ischemic heart disease in 2016: 35% higher stroke risk, 17% higher heart disease mortality versus 35-to-40-hour weeks. That is the case against long weeks, not proof that shorter weeks improve output.

Service quality, staffing costs, work shifted to nonparticipants and output per paid hour need to be measured together. The case for a gain is strongest where organizations can remove low-value meetings or reallocate work and weakest where continuous coverage requires replacement labor; the retrieved employee interviews identify coordination and workload concerns in such roles (Jain et al., 2025). ## What the Trials Changed Before They Cut the Day

The companies that made four-day weeks work did not just cross Friday off the calendar. They redesigned how work happened first.

Microsoft Japan capped meetings at 30 minutes. Fan et al. describe "pre-trial work reorganization" in which companies improved efficiency and collaboration before the six-month clock started. The common thread: fewer meetings, async communication, and protected focus blocks. These are the changes Parkinson's law predicts: work expands to fill the time, so when you cut the time, you cut the filler.

Whether your company runs four days or five, the practical lesson is the same. Your output tracks your focused hours, not your logged hours. Protecting two or three deep work blocks per day from meetings and interruptions is the part of these trials any schedule can copy, even if the headline was about the missing Friday. ## Frequently Asked Questions

### Is a 4 day work week 32 hours?

Usually, but not always. The 100-80-100 model tested in the UK pilot and Fan et al. means about 32 hours at full pay. A compressed 4x10 schedule keeps total hours at 40. Tokyo's public-sector model uses 155 hours per month. Same label, different hours.

### Which companies have a 4 day work week?

Microsoft Japan trialed it for one month in August 2019. The Tokyo Metropolitan Government began offering a compressed option in April 2025. Beyond those, the best-documented examples are the 61 UK pilot firms (56 intended to continue) and the 141 volunteer organizations in Fan et al., mostly white-collar and recruited through 4 Day Week Global.

### Do you get paid the same on a 4 day work week?

In the 100-80-100 model, yes. Workers take a 20% reduction in hours with no cut in pay. The compressed 4x10 model also preserves full pay since total hours remain at 40. Both the UK pilot and Fan et al. held wages constant.

### Is a 4x10 schedule better than five 8-hour days?

Bambra's 2008 review found that compressed weeks improved work-life balance, but the studies were low quality and outcomes were mostly self-reported. A 10-hour day can bring more fatigue, and childcare logistics can be harder. Whether it is "better" depends on your role, your commute, and how well you sustain focus past hour eight.

### Did productivity drop in the four-day week trials?

Revenue in the 23 UK firms that reported it rose 1.4% on average. Fan et al. measured well-being, not revenue. Microsoft Japan's 39.9% jump was one company, one month, with concurrent changes. Output mostly held steady where measured, but it was not measured in most trials.

### Is the US moving to a 32-hour work week?

The Thirty-Two-Hour Workweek Act (S. 3947) was introduced in the Senate in March 2024. It would phase the FLSA overtime threshold down from 40 to 32 hours. It has not advanced beyond introduction and is not law. No federal policy change is imminent as of 2026.
